Move the benchmark numbers into logbooks
items.body:
Numbers lived in whichever page argued from them, so the same figure appeared in two or
three places and none of them named the machine. That is exactly how `benchmarks.md`
reported 70 µs for a store write for months while measuring a store weft does not ship.

## One logbook per plane

Every measured number now lives under `docs/reference/`, with the apparatus, the method,
and the outcome:

| logbook | holds |
| --- | --- |
| `control_plane_logbook.md` | **new** — store backends, actor ops |
| `data_plane_logbook.md` | **new** — ring tiers, decode/apply, SUMO, zstd, iceoryx2, loopback |
| `store_plane_logbook.md` | existed — plus the local-file comparison and the pragma result |

Each keeps the runs that turned out to be **invalid**, and says why:

- the store bench that measured `Store.Sqlite` instead of `Store.Replicated`, wrong by 288x;
- the loopback receive test, where `recvmmsg` matching `recv` was the tell that it measured
  the send side;
- the 2500-candidate crash search that never finished.

A run that is deleted teaches nothing twice.

## The essay keeps the arguments

`benchmarks.md` is rewritten around the three results that moved a decision, two of which
moved it away from where we expected:

- the store we measured was not the store we ship, and on that host **a local fsync was
  slower than the network database**;
- compute was never the bottleneck, so the pessimistic DRAM number matters more than the
  fast cache-hot one;
- the message-passing ceiling was the copy, so the fix was to stop copying.

Tables also moved out of `runtime-choice.md` and `how-it-works.md`. What stays in the
essays is the reasoning and a pointer.

Two tables in `docs/essays/` are **not** measurements and stay put: the glossary in
`how-it-works.md` and the latency **budget** in `topology.md`, which is derived from human
perception rather than measured.

`CLAUDE.md` now states the split, so the next measurement lands in the right place.

The harness landed in #97. This attaches its output to the PR instead of leaving it on whoever's laptop ran it last — which is what the issue asks for: *"Nothing in this issue should be optimized without a number before and after."*

The harness already reports the **minimum** of several runs rather than the mean, which is what makes a number off a shared runner worth reading at all — noise only ever adds time, so the minimum converges on the work while the mean tracks the runner.

items.title: fix(docs): reconcile drifted benchmark numbers across all doc surfaces
items.body:
## Description

Audited every benchmark/economics claim in the repo against the code and evals that actually produce them, and closed the gaps found. No feature work — every number below was re-derived from a fresh, verified run against the final merged code, not guessed or copy-edited.

**Note on how this PR evolved:** the first commit fixed numbers measured against this branch's code. While preparing to push, the PR turned out to have a real merge conflict — `main` had drifted 985 commits ahead (several releases, substantial retrieval-path changes) and had independently drifted some of the *same* doc numbers on its own. Rather than resolve the conflict by picking one side, the second commit merges `main` in and **re-runs all three verification suites against the final merged code**, then propagates those numbers — which in some cases differ from what the first commit measured. The figures below are the current, final state.

**Economics (~1.6-3x, not 3-10x).** `docs/BUSINESS-CASE.md`'s own worked example already correctly derives ~1.6x end-to-end cost reduction, but 4 other surfaces (`HONEST-ASSESSMENT.md`, `about.html`, `Limits-and-Failure-Modes.md`, `vs-headroom.md`) still said "3-10x" — one of them self-contradicting its own page. Propagated the correct figure, and added an explicit disclosure that `neuralmind savings` (real logged usage vs. a fixed baseline) and `BUSINESS-CASE.md`'s formula (a what-if projection) are different measurements by design.

**Synapse-recall A/B (77.2%→83.3%, +6.1 pts).** Docs cited a stale "71.7%→83.3%, +11.6/+11.7 pts" in 16 files. A fresh run against the final merged code gives 77.2%→83.3%, +6.1 pts, deterministically — matching what `main` already had independently. Propagated everywhere. Also caught and fixed a real conflation: several surfaces mislabeled this synapse-recall delta as the *onboarding-lift* eval's number.

**Onboarding-lift eval (+0.9 pts, down from a previously-measured +6.5).** This is the most consequential finding. `evals/onboarding/runner.py` measures how much a committed team memory improves retrieval versus a cold agent — described in its own README as NeuralMind's "headline differentiator." Against this branch's pre-merge code it measured +6.5 pts (75.9%→82.4%). Against the fully merged code it's **+0.9 pts (81.5%→82.4%)** — the cold-path baseline itself got substantially better on `main`, which is a good thing architecturally, but it shrinks the memory layer's marginal contribution. Both measurements were real and deterministic at the time; noted honestly in `docs/wiki/Benchmarks.md` and `docs/wiki/Home.md` rather than smoothed over. Still clears the CI gate (lift ≥ 0).

**Public benchmark (79-100% recall, not a flat 100%).** `bench/public/report.md`/`results.json` were generated once at the benchmark's original commit and never regenerated since, despite `evals/public/manifest.json` growing to 4 repos (`requests`/`click`/`flask`/`rich`, 40 queries). Reran `python -m evals.public.run` against the final merged code: aggregate is **79-100% gold-file recall (93.75% mean, 90% found-rate), 44.9x-256.8x fewer tokens**. Also corrected an unconditional "beats ripgrep on both recall and cost" claim — NeuralMind ties ripgrep's recall exactly on `click` and `rich` (still wins cost on all 4). `click` is now the weakest repo (2 misses of 7) where an earlier run had zero — rewrote `docs/benchmarks/public.md`'s "Where NeuralMind loses" and "The corpus" sections to report this plainly, including the meta-point that this page's numbers moved twice in the same audit. Logged the regenerate-on-drift gap in `ROADMAP.md`.

**Left untouched, flagged instead of guessed:** the separate `codebase-memory-mcp` competitor-eval MRR numbers (off-by-default, needs an external binary this session didn't install) — noted inline in `public.md` as not yet re-verified against the expanded corpus.

## Type of Change

- [x] 📝 Documentation update

## How Has This Been Tested?

All verification below was run against the **final merged code** (after merging `main`):

- `python scripts/check_commercial_terms.py` — passes.
- `black --check` / `ruff check` on touched Python files (`neuralmind/cli.py`, `neuralmind/savings.py`, `neuralmind/__init__.py` — docstring/comment/version-conflict-resolution only, no logic changes) — pass.
- `pytest tests/test_benchmark_regression.py -v` — 5/5 pass.

- Every changed number was independently regenerated against the merged code: `python -m tests.benchmark.run` (4x, deterministic), `python -m evals.onboarding.runner --run` (3x, deterministic), `python -m evals.public.run` (full 4-repo run).
- Manual repo-wide `git grep` sweep after each fix confirmed no stale instances of the old numbers remain outside `docs/releases/` (historical, intentionally exempt) and `CHANGELOG.md`.

### Test Configuration

items.body:
Re-measured for 6.0 on the same instance type and CPU as the numbers they replace (AWS c7i.large, Xeon Platinum 8488C, 2 vCPU), same methodology (synthetic suite, 1000 ms/task, 500 ms cooldown, median of 3 runs), Node v22.23.2, Ajv 8.20.0, at commit `2cd9140`.

## Validate: unchanged

Within run-to-run noise, and the prose holds. The only edit is the fast-fail rejection range widening from 84-87% to 84-94%.

## Compile: regressed, and the table now says so

| shape | published (`6270795`) | measured (`2cd9140`) | speedup then / now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tiny` | 27.4 us | 39.6 us | 285x / 199x |
| `petstore` | 132.1 us | 180.8 us | 51x / 37x |
| `tree` | 70.0 us | 132.4 us | 101x / 50x |
| `composition` | 297.9 us | 429.5 us | 24x / 16x |
| `array-heavy` | 97.7 us | 141.6 us | 68x / 46x |
| `unique-primitives` | 41.1 us | 55.2 us | 149x / 109x |
| `long-string` | 73.5 us | 98.1 us | 86x / 61x |

**Ajv is the control and moved 1-6% on the same host**, so this is the code, not the machine.

Cause is compile-time work accumulated across the cycle. `packages/schema/src` took 3662 insertions in that window, four of them lint passes that run by default (#547, #551, #620, #684). Profiled locally:

| cost per `compileSchema` | `tiny` | `tree` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| schema-lint passes (default `warn`) | 6.6 us (50%) | 13.8 us (57%) |
| re-normalizing the `formats` map | 8.2 us | 7.3 us |

Filed as #702 (lint cost) and #701 (formats re-normalization). Neither is a correctness problem and neither blocked the release, so this publishes the measured numbers rather than the flattering ones.

The claim the section actually makes survives: compile stays an order of magnitude or two ahead of Ajv.

## Also

- The `long-string` cells stay capped at `>1000x`, with the footnote carrying the detail. The measured multipliers are four and five digits; spelling them out made the row read like a headline number rather than the shape-specific artefact it is.
- Memory re-measured. Steady RSS, heap and throughput land where they did. Baseline RSS is the one row that moved (eov now lower than oaverify rather than higher); the prose makes no baseline claim and still reads true.

Raw host-stamped JSON stays gitignored per `performance/README.md`.

items.title: Survive write-only credentials, and publish real-S3 benchmark numbers
items.body:
## Summary

The real-bucket benchmark run, and the bug it found before it could even start.

## The bug

The provided credentials were scoped write-only (`PutObject`/`List`/`Delete`, no `GetObject`) — a legitimate CI shape. `s3lfs track` crashed: the upload path's ETag skip-check calls `HeadObject`, which requires `s3:GetObject`, and the resulting 403 aborted the upload. The check now degrades to uploading — worst case is re-sending bytes that already exist. Tested with a mocked 403.

The harness gains `--upload-only` for such credentials.

## The numbers (real AWS S3, us-west-2, 201 MB, vs s5cmd v2.3.0)

| scenario | s3lfs | s5cmd |
|---|---|---|
| cold upload, incompressible | 3.1s | 2.1s |
| cold upload, **compressible** | **1.0s** | 2.2s |
| re-run, nothing changed | 0.2s | 0.1s |
| one file of 24 changed | 0.9s | 0.4s |

Three findings worth stating plainly:

1. **The localhost numbers overstated the gap badly.** 3–10× locally becomes **1.5×** on a real network — the per-file costs mostly disappear into the transfer.
2. **On compressible data s3lfs wins outright, 2.2×**, because it sends ~1% of the bytes.
3. **CRT made no measurable difference** for this workload (3.16s with, 3.07–3.17s without, across three runs). The remaining gap to s5cmd is s3lfs's own per-file work — hashing (0.5 ms/MB, the price of content addressing) and the staging copy — not the HTTP engine. The staging copy is the next optimization candidate if 1.5× still matters.

Classic-engine repeatability across runs was 3.07/3.17/3.16 — tight enough to trust the comparisons.

All 196 benchmark objects were deleted from the bucket afterward; `s3lfs-bench/` is empty.

## Testing

New test: upload survives a denied HeadObject. 896 passed, 3 skipped; pre-commit clean.

items.title: docs: drop benchmark numbers from the JDK caching section
items.body:
**Description:**

The JDK caching section in `docs/advanced-usage.md` quoted specific benchmark timings (median warm `setup-java` falling from 7s to 3s, median warm job from 24s to 18s, 175.3 MiB of storage) and linked an external benchmark repository. This removes both.

Point-in-time measurements do not belong in reference documentation. They come from one runner type, one distribution, one JDK size, and one project, and they go stale silently as runner images, vendor CDNs, and the action itself change. A reader has no way to tell how far their situation is from the measured one, so a concrete number invites being read as a guarantee rather than as one data point. The external repository link has the same problem in reverse: it points readers away from the reference docs to something they then have to interpret.

What replaces it is the part that stays true regardless of environment: a warm run restores the installed JDK instead of downloading, verifying, and extracting it; the first run pays to upload it; and every cached identity consumes repository cache storage. The existing guidance about which factors drive the result (runner, distribution, JDK size, network, cache eviction pressure) is kept.

The billed-minutes aside was also dropped. It described how GitHub bills job time rather than anything about `setup-java`, so it belonged in the Actions billing documentation rather than here.

## Summary

The research design asks that the latest numbers be published so a visitor can compare without running anything. `docs/benchmarks/` held only prose, so there was nothing for a reader to compare or a contributor to beat.

`scripts/run_benchmarks.py` runs every manifest and generates the results page: a metric table, and per benchmark its seed, backend, manifest digest, and every scenario's expected versus observed outcome. items.title: feat(decisions): declared note supersession + published benchmark numbers
items.body:
Two related changes: notes can finally record that one supersedes another, and the two
decision-log suites now publish real numbers instead of "No accepted local checkpoint".

## Why `**Amends:**` had zero uses across 181 notes

Not neglect — **notes had no identity to point at.** `retrieval.mts` minted note ids as
`note:<date>` with no occurrence suffix, so on the axis carrying six notes dated `2026-07-03`,
all six answered to the same id. The `**Amends:**` marker has existed since sc-1236 as a bare
flag with nothing after it, because there was nothing it *could* name.

Measured on the real corpus: **~25% of notes supersede an earlier note on their own axis**, and
nothing recorded which one won — retrieval served the superseded note and its correction as
equally-weighted qualifiers on the same ruling.

## Declared, not detected

The pointer is declared by the writer and validated by the gate. Detection was measured dead: a
narrow supersede/reverse grep recovers 25% of the real cases while a broader one overshoots to
48%, because notes use reversal vocabulary precisely to *deny* they are reversals ("not a
reversal", "reconfirms"). Separating a genuine supersession from a refinement needs a note read
against its predecessor — an LLM call the commit gate cannot make. That stays in the offline
benchmark, where a wrong answer costs a report line rather than a blocked commit.

- **Identity** — `note:<date>~N`, minted **once** in `recall/note-relations.mts` and imported by
  both retrieval and the gate. `supersession.mts` learned this the hard way for Targets: two
  independent minters drift, a valid reference reads as dangling, and the gate cries wolf.
- **Declaration** — `--supersedes <id>` on `add --note` renders `**Amends:** <id> — <text>`. One
  verb across both levels; the flag was already parsed and silently ignored on the note path, so
  this costs zero new lines in `decisions.mts` (which sits at its 500-line cap).
- **Validation** — at the **write** path *and* as integrity check #8. sc-1282 shipped the opposite
  bug and had to fix it: a CLI that writes records its own check rejects.

**Fires 0/181 on both real corpora** (146 frink + 35 devkit) — no grandfathering, unlike the
mandatory-relation-tag proposal that died firing 36/36.

Adding check #8 immediately failed the save-quality bench on `checksUncovered` — the mechanism
from sc-1282 correctly refusing a check with no perturbation case. A fixture, mutation and case
row were required before it would go green.

## Published benchmark numbers

The dashboard machinery already worked; these two suites simply had no baseline file for
`publish` to read. Added a generic **`deterministic` adapter**: every existing adapter
reverse-engineers metrics out of a bespoke LLM-judge shape, but a suite that *counts* rather than
*judges* already knows its numbers, so the baseline is just
`{metrics: [{id, label, k, n}], rows, floorsMet}`. Reusable by any future counting suite.

| suite | published |
|---|---|
| Decision-log save quality | Defect recall **13/13 (100%)** · FPR@R80 **0/18 (0%)** · checks exercised 8/8 · real records clean 34/34 |
| Decision-log retrieval recall | Gold axis retrieved **11/12 (91.7%)** · set recall **2/4 (50%)** · current-state accuracy 6/6 · **answered-when-should-abstain 11/11** |

Failures are published deliberately. Abstention is excluded from `floorsMet` because it is a
known-open axis — the number is there so it can move, not to gate on day one. A dashboard that
only shows wins is an advertisement, not an instrument.

Recall is published against the **lexical tier** (`DECISIONS_NO_EMBED=1`), which is what CI runs —
a hybrid number would be irreproducible without Ollama and `nomic-embed-text`, and a figure nobody
else can regenerate is not evidence.

Both suites stay `lifecycle: experimental`. One checkpoint is not a trend.

## Validation

- `bun run typecheck`, `npx eslint gate-engine`, `npx biome check` — clean (2 pre-existing warnings)
- decisions + eval suites: **420 passed**
- `benchmarks:check` — `PASS (working)`
- save-quality bench exit 0; `guard-decisions integrity` clean beyond the one known exception

## Bug found, not fixed here

`publish --tree WORKTREE` refuses with *"requires a completely clean working tree"* on a
verifiably clean tree — `git status --porcelain=v1 --untracked-files=all` returns 0 bytes, and
reproducing its exact `spawnSync` call from node gives the same empty result. `--tree HEAD` works,
so that is what these checkpoints used. Worth its own ticket: `--tree WORKTREE` is the path the
sc-1236 handover documents, so it will bite again.

items.title: 📝 State the conditions the benchmark numbers were measured under
items.body:
Closes #637.

The issue asked for the published numbers to be re-run on a clean machine. It also asked whether that is the right bar at all. It is not, so this changes the bar rather than chasing it.

## Why the bar changed

A cleanliness claim is unverifiable from the outside. A reader cannot tell whether the machine was idle, and has no reason to take our word for it, so the claim buys credibility it cannot back. Meanwhile the page already says the right thing twice: the numbers are indicative, and the scripts are runnable on your own hardware. That is the actual offer.

So the page now states what it can prove: hardware, interpreter, dates, and the conditions the run happened under, including that the machine was shared.

| | |
|---|---|
| Hardware | Apple Silicon, macOS |
| Interpreter | CPython 3.12 |
| Measured | 2026-06-14, circuit breaker rows 2026-07-29 |
| Conditions | Developer machine, shared with other work |

It also says plainly that a quiet machine would move the figures, and not evenly across rows, and points the reader at their own baseline instead of this table.

The numbers themselves are unchanged. Re-running them today would have produced worse ones under the same caveat: this machine sat at a load average of 4.6 when I checked, and touched 35 during a full test run. Publishing fresh figures measured under that, dated today, would look more authoritative while being less true.

## Launch checklist

The item is ticked with the reasoning recorded, since it documents a decision rather than a task done. That was the last unchecked box: **the pre-launch section is now complete.**

items.title: feat(client): tree-shakeable boot features, docs overhaul, honest benchmark numbers
items.body:
## Summary

Follows up on #93. Three things: the bundle-size regression is fixed, the docs are current and reorganized after surveying other frameworks, and the benchmark numbers published in README/docs match reality again.

### fix: bundle regression (24.7 → 34.8KB crept, now 30.9KB gzip)

`boot({ glow: true, cursor: true })` bundled the glow painter, the simulated cursor, the i18n installer and the query cache into every app — used or not. Each layer added between 0.4.0 and 0.6.0 wired itself unconditionally into `boot()`, growing the krausest fixture from 24.7 to 34.8KB js_gzip, past the `js_gzip ≤ 0.5×react` ratio guard.

Boot features are now **code the app imports, not flags**:

```ts
import { boot, agentGlow, agentCursor, i18n } from 'janux/client';

boot({ defs: [App], glow: agentGlow(), cursor: agentCursor(), i18n: i18n() });
```

- `glow` / `cursor` take `agentGlow(options?)` / `agentCursor(options?)` (`BootFeature`); `true` is a type error and dev builds warn at runtime.
- New `i18n: i18n()` feature reads the page dictionary and re-reads it after every SPA navigation (previously unconditional — i18n apps must now pass it).
- Query-payload hydration moved from `boot()` into the first browser `getQueryClient()`; the `window.__JANUX_QUERY__` sink semantics are unchanged, SSR data is still never refetched.
- The always-on WebMCP surface keeps its paint primitives through the new `client/feedback.ts` seam; `enableAgentGlow`/`enableAgentCursor` remain for manual wiring.
- The package declares `"sideEffects": false`, so re-exported-but-unused modules (the SSR unsuspense runtime among them) drop out of client builds.

**Measured** (deterministic bytes, 2026-08-06): js_gzip 34,818 → **30,937** (react 62,120; 0.560 → **0.498×**), fw_gzip 32,843 → **28,963** (0.482×). Both bundle guards green; a full 19-suite verification run kept all 23 ratio guards green. All 39 example/template call sites migrated; changeset included; BASELINE log entry #26.

### docs: currency pass + framework-style reorganization

- **The compiler finally has a home** beyond one roadmap bullet: a `compiler` row (plus 6 other missing fields: `fonts`, `redirects`, `rewrites`, `navigation`, `cache`, `serviceWorker`) in the config reference, both passes documented in `build-internals`, binding-maps paragraphs in `views-and-jsx` and the mental model, a FAQ entry, and glossary terms.
- **Boot features documented** across `client-api`, `client-runtime` (new Agent feedback section), `events-and-interactions`, the i18n guide and the monorepo recipe — export-coverage guard satisfied for every new export.
- **Reorganization**: after surveying next.js, svelte, nuxt, fresh, qwik and brisa, the IA already matches the field, so no mass moves (571 internal links are test-guarded). Surgical changes only: `guide/getting-started.md` → `guide/overview.md` (name collided with the getting-started *section*), the sidebar's "Testing & deployment" group splits so deployment is a findable destination, and two parity-gap pages are new: `more/upgrading.md` and `reference/errors.md` (grounded in the actual runtime messages).
- **Counts fixed**: 43 runnable examples (README said 34), 114 pages, 11,954 tests; duplicate example link in README removed.

### docs(bench): numbers match the current state

- Shipped-bytes tables re-quote the 2026-08-06 deterministic measurement (janux **30.9KB** vs react 62.1 · preact 10.0 · solid 14.1 · svelte 18.4 · vue-vapor 24.1).
- Fixed a factually wrong claim: "typing into 512 controlled fields: 16.84ms vs 45.58" was actually `scaling-curves update_512`; the real `controlled-form typing` row (janux 83.2ms vs react 49.1 — a loss) is relabeled and moved to the honest-gaps list.
- Ratio-guard notes in `baselines/ratios.json` now state the recorded 0.498/0.482 and why the thin headroom is deliberate.

## Test plan

- [x] Full suite: **11,954 pass / 0 fail** (packages, docs-tests, apps/docs, example suites, scripts)
- [x] `bun run typecheck` green across all packages, 43 examples and 3 templates
- [x] e2e: green (2 initial failures were an unbuilt example in a fresh worktree; 7/7 after building it)

items.title: bench(ci): workflow for publishable benchmark numbers
items.body:
The published README and `docs/performance/` figures predate this round of optimizations, and were produced ad hoc on a developer machine with Mountebank taken from whoever happened to have it installed. This makes producing them reproducible.

## What it guarantees

**Mountebank is pinned and installed by the workflow** (`mountebank@2.9.1` by default, an input). The comparison only means something if both engines are the same versions every time.

**Every published cell is a median with its spread stated.** #746 published a figure from a single rep that landed on a degraded runner and had to be retracted; `--rep` plus the aggregation step makes that structurally impossible rather than a matter of discipline.

**The host is recorded in the artefact.** Absolute numbers are machine-specific, so the report says which machine produced them.

## Two phases

1. **Comparison** — both engines, same rep count, aggregated with `--aggregate-comparison`, which refuses unequal replication between engines.
2. **Rift-only sweep** — connection scaling (1/50/256/512) plus the matching-dimension scenarios the comparison set deliberately excludes, since that set is a stability contract with previously published numbers.

## A collision I caught before shipping it

Both phases write `direct_rift_repN.csv` — same engine, same empty variant suffix — so the sweep would have **silently overwritten the comparison's inputs**, and the published table would have been built from whichever survived. That is the #773 overwrite class reintroduced one layer up, in the workflow rather than the harness.

The comparison artefacts are now parked in `results/comparison/` before the sweep runs.

Manual dispatch only: these figures go into user-facing docs, so producing them should be deliberate.

Refs #702, #773.

## Method

## Results (Rust ×mongod, was → now)

| Workload | mongod | Rust | ×mongod | Python | ×mongod |
|---|---:|---:|:---:|---:|:---:|
| insert | 60.9 ms | 77.5 ms | 1.3× (1.6×) | 298.7 ms | 4.9× |

items.title: perf(po): allocation-focused catalog speedups and refreshed benchmark numbers
items.body:
## Summary

Two profiling-driven optimization rounds over the catalog hot paths, each candidate implemented in an isolated worktree, validated for byte-identical output, and only kept when a sequential benchmark on the reference host (Apple M1 Ultra) showed a real improvement.

Published numbers move from this morning's baseline to:

| Workload | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| Full catalog update (`po-update/gettext-ui-de-10000`) | 112 MiB/s | **150 MiB/s** (+33%) |
| Update with new strings (`po-merge`) | 255 MiB/s | **291 MiB/s** (+14%) |
| Borrowed parse | 695 MiB/s | **725 MiB/s** |
| ICU-heavy update (internal) | ~97 MiB/s | ~144 MiB/s (+48%) |

The full-update lead over the fastest non-Ferrocat workflow update grows from 2.4x to 3.4x, and over GNU `msgmerge` to ~31x.

## Round 1 — allocation churn (samply showed 26% malloc + 15% memmove)

- `perf(po): drop throwaway sets in catalog merge helpers` — in-place dedup/compaction, `FxHashSet` for membership only, fast paths for empty/small inputs; new equivalence test against a naive reference across all size paths
- `perf(po): drop redundant buffers in catalog message import` — halves the catalog layer's own allocations on top of the parser; documents the in-place-collect size coupling between `CanonicalMessage` and the public `CatalogMessage`
- `perf(po): parse catalogs through the borrowed PO parser` — the catalog path consumes `parse_po_borrowed`, allocating each retained field exactly once; also fixes a pre-existing owned/borrowed parser divergence on irregular header blocks (validated with a 1.04M-input mutation differential, four regression tests)
- `perf(po): cut allocation churn in plural synthesis and PO export` — exact-size plural synthesis buffers, borrowed category tables (`&'static str`), presized serializer output
- `perf(po): cut per-message allocations in catalog export` — allocation-free placeholder-comment scan, origins rendered straight into the output buffer, per-operation gettext plural profile cache
- `perf(po): move each message once when applying collated order` — scatter through a scratch buffer instead of swap cycles, identity early-return

## Round 2 — after re-profiling the optimized build

- `perf(bench): ingest templates via the borrowed PO parser` — the compare harness parses `template.pot` zero-copy in the update and merge scenarios; conversion pinned byte-exactly against the previous owned conversion
- `perf(po): move merged message payloads instead of cloning` — identity matching as a separate pass, matched messages taken by value, `unchanged`/`changed` stats decided field-by-field instead of comparing against a retained clone (128-configuration differential: byte-identical output, stats, and diagnostics)
- `perf(po): continue collation prefixes on collision` — colliding 32-byte prefix buckets are re-keyed at offsets 32/64/96 before any full key is built (provably order-preserving; eliminates the full-key degeneration on Lingui-style offset-plural catalogs, 4000 -> 0 in the probe corpus). Same-msgid runs skip continuation entirely, which keeps ICU-heavy catalogs with repeated msgids at baseline speed.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --all-features --locked`, `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`, `cargo +1.93.0 check` (MSRV) — all green
- The compare suite's semantic-equivalence digests are unchanged against every recorded report, so output parity is verified against msgmerge, pofile, pofile-ts, polib, and Babel
- Published numbers are backed by three new checked-in reports at `c3caa27` and validated by `scripts/check-published-numbers.mjs` (18 values, 14 swept mentions); ADR 0026 keeps its historical collation measurements pinned to their original reports

## Notes for review

- The last four commits are unsigned (1Password signing agent was locked during the session); the earlier commits are signed as usual
- A pre-existing FCL bug surfaced during differential testing (plural entries round-tripped through FCL trip a spurious duplicate-id conflict on re-merge, reproducible on the baseline) — tracked separately, not addressed here

items.title: docs(performance): refresh benchmark numbers on two hosts
items.body:
The published benchmark figures predated the Turbo optimization round, so the one
result that round actually moved was invisible.

## What moved

`regex_last` went from **54,434 → 207,024 RPS** on comparable hardware. It used to be
Rift's only slow path — the one predicate type that can't be hash-dispatched — and the
candidate-bitset matching framework brought it in line with everything else. Mountebank
went 106 → 112 over the same period, so the gap widened from 515x to **1,857x** because
Rift improved, not because Mountebank regressed. Every page now says that explicitly;
"1,857x" on its own invites the wrong inference.

## Two hosts, not one headline

| | Apple M4 laptop | AMD EPYC 9V74, 16 vCPU |
|---|--:|--:|
| Rift, simple stub | 214,818 | 324,952 |
| Mountebank, simple stub | 8,898 | **5,982** |
| Regex, 100th pattern | 1,857x | 6,160x |

Going to the server **Rift speeds up and Mountebank slows down** — it is single-threaded
and this server's individual cores are slower than the M4's, so it gains nothing from the
other 15. The EPYC multipliers are therefore inflated at *both* ends. Publishing only the
6,160x figure would not survive scrutiny, so both columns ship together and each page
states which is the conservative read (the M4 — still 22x–1,857x).

## Honesty caveats now published, not buried

- Every figure is a **median of 3 repetitions**, reproducible via `--rep N` +
  `--aggregate-comparison`.
- **M4 figures carry ~±10%.** Both engines lost ~7% aggregate between the first and last
  repetition — a laptop thermally throttling over a 30-minute run. Per-scenario spread
  reached 12% on M4 vs 5% on EPYC. Stated inline with the reason.
- Tail latency is the more stable comparison and is included: Rift p99 **0.43–0.97 ms on
  both hosts**; Mountebank 2.9 ms to 1.7 *seconds*.

## Provenance

- EPYC: `benchmark-publish.yml` run [29767296487](https://github.com/achird-labs/rift/actions/runs/29767296487), c=50, 20s, 3 reps.
- M4: local run on a quiesced machine, same harness/flags/versions, 3 reps.
- Both: Rift `master` @ `924cf73`, Mountebank `2.9.1`, `oha`, native processes, each engine alone.

Docs-only — no code touched. `verify-docs-coverage.sh` green.

items.title: Describe performance qualitatively instead of quoting benchmark numbers (#52a)
items.body:
Phase 2 of the #47 epic, covering the messaging-precision half of #52.

The homepage advertised **"60× faster · 22× less RAM · 100 TB queryable from a laptop"** and *"no downloads, no decoders, no waiting"*. Re-running the benchmark showed every one of those needed work — and the fix turned out not to be a better number, but not putting an environment-dependent number on a banner at all.

## Why the speedup number had to go

Six runs of the same notebook on one machine:

```
43×   50.8×   65×   103×   125×   145×
```

That spread is network variance in the file-based download loop, not a property of the software. Any figure we publish is really a statement about our laptop's S3 throughput that afternoon. `docs/tutorials.md` had independently claimed "~6 min vs ~10 s", so the site also contradicted itself.

The site now states what is invariably true — **hours of preparation become seconds of analysis** — and [Notebook 3](https://atmoscale.github.io/radar-datatree/3.QVP-Workflow-Comparison.html) measures the actual ratio on the reader's machine and prints it. The wording follows [atmoscale.ai](https://atmoscale.ai/) ("From hours of preparation to seconds of analysis") so both sites read as one voice.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| speed | `60× faster than file-based` | `Hours → seconds` · preparation becomes analysis |
| data | `22× less RAM` | `Open formats` · Zarr v3 · Icechunk · no lock-in |
| size | `100 TB queryable from a laptop` | `One dataset` · every VCP and sweep, time-indexed |

## The other three claims

**"22× less RAM" was never a memory measurement.** It is `data_reduction` — a byte ratio of decoded volumes against streamed chunks, stable to four decimals because it is structural rather than environmental, and resting on a nominal 4:1 Level II compression assumption. Worth knowing: **atmoscale.ai quotes "5.8× less data"**, which is the *wire* ratio for this same benchmark, while ours was the *decoded* ratio. Both are now off the banner and explained in the glossary instead.

**"100 TB queryable from a laptop"** understated the logical size — Notebook 1 prints 167 TB for KLOT alone and it grows — while overstating what a laptop holds, since it fetches the few hundred MB a query touches.

**"no downloads, no decoders, no waiting"** was literally false: queries move bytes and some paths still decode. Replaced with the distinction that is actually true — *no bulk downloads, no file-by-file decoding, no manual archive assembly* — as #52 asks.

## New glossary section

`docs/glossary.md` gains **"How big is the archive?"**, separating the five numbers people call "size": logical, compressed source, materialized, virtual reference, and bytes actually transferred. It keeps the concrete figures (809 MiB on the wire, ~3.2 GB decoded, 146 MB actually needed) where a reader looking for evidence will find them, framed as a worked example rather than a banner claim. Phase 3's #48 benchmark will fill it with measured values.

## Two things an audit caught that would otherwise have shipped

- An earlier draft of this very change published **">50× faster"** as a floor. The build open in front of me already printed **43.2×** — below the floor and outside the disclosed range, on the exact page cited as proof.
- `scripts/generate_social_card.py` still baked **"60× faster / 22× less RAM"** into `docs/_static/social-card.png`, which `docs/conf.py` wires as `og:image`. Every Slack and LinkedIn preview advertised the two strings this PR removes. Regenerated; the phrase moved to the tagline after longer strings overflowed the fixed metric grid (verified by looking at the rendered PNG, not just the script's exit code).

## Left alone deliberately

Notebook 4's "112× to 1,565×" is explicitly attributed to the paper's 30-worker cluster run, not to anything that notebook demonstrates. Its own tables imply a different range — that discrepancy is a question about the paper's numbers, not something to silently rewrite here.

## Verification

`ruff check` / `ruff format --check` / `black --check` pass on all tracked files; docs build succeeds with zero warnings; no numeric performance claim remains anywhere on the site.

## Note for sequencing

This branches from merged `main`, independent of #55. Both touch `notebooks/3.QVP-Workflow-Comparison.ipynb` but in different cells (#55 makes the QVP definition a visible section; this rewrites the TL;DR), so they merge cleanly — whichever lands second just wants a rebase check.

items.title: feat(bench): phyz-bench harness with published, honest benchmark numbers
items.body:
Adds a reproducible benchmark harness so phyz's performance claims are measurable rather than asserted — including the cases where phyz loses.

## What changed

- **`crates/phyz-bench`** — five suites over a shared set of scenes: single-sim throughput, GPU batch sweep, gradient cost, energy drift, and a like-for-like Rapier comparison. Machine metadata (CPU, OS, profile, git rev) is stamped into every run. Suites that can't run (no wgpu adapter, etc.) report `skipped` with a reason rather than failing.
- **`BENCHMARKS.md`** — published numbers recorded by hand from a known idle machine.
- **`Makefile`** — `make bench` for the publishable run, plus `bench-quick`, `bench-gpu`, `bench-criterion`, and pointers to the optional MuJoCo/MJX Python harness.
- **`.github/workflows/bench.yml`** — manual dispatch + weekly cron only. `continue-on-error`, never runs on push/PR.
- **README** — links BENCHMARKS.md and surfaces the two unflattering numbers up front.

## Why the CI workflow does not gate

Timing on shared GitHub runners is noisy: neighbours on the host, variable CPU models, no thermal guarantees. A gate built on that fails randomly, and a randomly-failing gate is one people learn to ignore. The workflow exists to prove the harness still compiles and runs end to end, and its artifacts are explicitly stamped as *not* publishable so a CI number can never be mistaken for a recorded one.

## For reviewers

Two results worth reading before adopting phyz, both documented rather than buried:

- The GPU path does not break even against a single CPU thread until roughly **batch 128**. Below that it is slower, substantially so at batch 1.
- Gradient rollouts cost **18–54×** a forward rollout, and the ratio grows with parameter count. The derivatives are *exact*, which is the real benefit — they are not asymptotically cheaper than finite differences today.

That second point has a follow-up already in flight (making adjoint gradient cost independent of param count); this PR measures the status quo, it does not fix it.

`cargo test -p phyz-bench` passes (8 tests, ~57s) — they check determinism, energy conservation to order dt, contact-force generation, and that skips serialise with reasons.

items.title: Make the published benchmark numbers honest
items.body:
## Purpose

The workspace publishes throughput numbers in its READMEs and posts A/B comparisons on pull requests. Several methodology flaws made those numbers misleading: single-op samples charged the operation for the per-iteration container teardown, the reported statistic was sensitive to outliers, two of the measured families never reached any published surface, and the CI A/B capture did nothing to separate a real change from slow machine drift. This makes the numbers trustworthy end to end, before the next time they are republished.

## Summary

- **Exclude container teardown from single-op timings.** The `remove`/`insert_*` single-op benches build a fresh container per iteration; the harness dropped that container *inside* the timed region, so every sample charged the operation for the container's destructor. Switched to `iter_batched_ref`, so teardown runs outside the measured window and each sample times only the operation.
- **Report the median with confidence bounds.** Ingest reads cargo-criterion's `median` estimate (with lower/upper bounds) instead of `typical`. The median is robust to the occasional cold-cache or scheduler outlier that skews a mean.
- **Surface every measured family.** The build/churn *workload* and pack/unpack *convert* families are measured on every run but were dropped from every published surface. They now appear in the README tables, the SVG charts, and the A/B delta table alongside the single-op family. (The trie family is the one remaining deferred surface — a small follow-up on this same tooling.)
- **Honest A/B comparison tooling.** `xtask compare` averages replicate captures per ref, marks any delta whose confidence interval overlaps the noise floor with `~`, and prints a non-failing "N of M deltas exceed noise" summary — a smoke signal for authors and reviewers, not a hard gate.
- **Drift-canceling full-precision captures.** Full-precision comparison runs capture each ref twice, interleaved base/head/head/base (A/B/B/A) on one runner. Both refs' captures center at the same point in the run, so a slow *linear* thermal/turbo drift cancels in the base-vs-head differential rather than biasing whichever ref was measured later. Quick PR runs stay single-pass (base once, head once): a fast smoke test whose ~30-min-per-capture cost is not worth doubling.

## Testing

- `just ci` green: clippy (pedantic/nursery, `-D warnings`) across the 140-config feature powerset, 144 nextest tests + doctests, and `cargo doc -D warnings`.
- `actionlint` clean on every touched workflow.

## Compatibility

No public API or crate source changed — this is bench-harness, `xtask` tooling, and CI only, so the `0.1.x` line is preserved.

## Documentation

No numeric republish here by design. The committed README tables and `docs/bench/*.svg` are intentionally **not** regenerated in this PR: the generators and their tests change, but the numbers are republished once — later, after the cross-crate inlining work — so they reflect that change exactly once rather than twice.

## Scope

Intentionally out of scope, tracked as follow-ups: surfacing the trie clone/drop family through the same three surfaces, and the single post-inlining numeric republish of the committed tables and charts.

items.title: docs(gfql): delete refuted and unverifiable benchmark numbers, and gate the rest
items.body:
> **Review-only. Do not self-merge.** Split out of #1806 at the owner's request: a wrong public number and badly-written prose have different urgencies, and bundling them made the urgent fix wait. This is the urgent half — **deletion and mechanism only, no editorial rewriting**. The prose rewrite is #PRB.

## What was wrong, and by how much

Two figures on `gfql/performance.rst` are not stale. They are wrong, and a matched, row-validated re-run on the same host says so:

| Published claim | Measured | |
|---|---|---|
| `performance.rst:145` — OLAP "q8 runs in **5.0 ms vs 1,004 ms** for embedded Kuzu (**200×**)" | q8 @100k: GFQL-polars **5.06 ms** vs Kuzu 0.11.3 **9.76 ms** = **1.93×** | **REFUTED**, off by ~100× |
| `performance.rst:146` — OLAP "q9 is **14.2×**" | q9 @100k: **66.61 ms** vs **84.06 ms** = **1.26×** | **REFUTED**, off by ~11× |

The 1,004 ms Kuzu figure is a historical board that pyg-bench's own results file records as *"did not reproduce and cannot be reproduced"* — a competitor handicap. It was still on the public docs.

## What could not be defended, and is therefore gone

Two of these are worse than unverifiable:

- **`engines.rst`'s LadybugDB column (65× / 1.2× / 3.5–3.7×)** traces to `benchmarks/gfql/bench_ladybug_cypher.py:52`, which **hardcodes `LADYBUG = {...}` with no URL, no version, no citation**. That is a literal, not a measurement of a competitor. It can never be published. The whole head-to-head is withdrawn, including the uncited "1.8B-edge graph in <8 GB RAM" figure attached to the same row.
- **`benchmark_filter_pagerank.rst`'s two committed SVG charts** are produced by `benchmarks/gfql/filter_pagerank/presentation.py:18`, which reads `plans/gfql-gpu-pagerank-benchmark/results/` — a path that **has never existed in any commit**. Nobody, including us, can regenerate them. The charts and the 46× / >56× / 8× / 54× / >26× figures they carry are removed, and the two SVG files are deleted.

The rest could be neither confirmed nor refuted. The reproducers wrote to `/tmp` or only printed, recorded no commit, host or timestamp, and their artifacts were never committed and no longer exist. `grep -l "rev-parse\|gethostname\|git_sha\|platform.node" benchmarks/gfql/*.py` returns nothing — **no GFQL benchmark runner records provenance at all**. Withdrawn on those grounds:

- the four-engine Orkut / LiveJournal bulk table and its CPU-crossover ratios (`performance.rst`, echoed in `engines.rst`)
- the 0.58.0 tag-sweep tables — seeded fast path, resident index, flat scaling (`performance.rst`, `indexing.rst`)
- the LDBC-SNB-vs-Neo4j table: every row that maps onto a query id the current lane emits differs materially from the current board **on both sides** (e.g. `seed-lookup` 106.1 → 28.08 ms on our side, 143.7 → 155.32 ms on Neo4j's), and `recent-replies` maps onto **no query id the current lane emits at all**, so it cannot be re-derived — only re-measured
- the seeded-index synthetic and vs-Kuzu/Neo4j tables and the prepared-Kuzu figures (`index_adjacency.rst`)
- every downstream echo: `~38x`, `9-28x vs Kuzu/Neo4j`, `43X+`, `10-50x`, `100X+`, `10X+`, plus the `~10K`-edge crossover, `100M+`, `80M+ output rows` and `<1 ms` thresholds that were outputs of the withdrawn runs

**`benchmark_graphframes.rst` is kept intact.** Its raw results are committed at `docs/source/gfql/_static/graphframes/results.json` and every headline cell round-trips against it. Bringing it under the gate is a follow-up.

This is a large removal. Removing an unverifiable number is a correct outcome, not a regression.

## The mechanism, so it does not recur

Docs no longer restate a number; they reference it.

- **`docs/source/_data/gfql_benchmarks.json`** — the single source of truth. Every cell names the run that produced it: measurement date, host, perf lock held, quiet host, rep protocol, frozen pygraphistry commit, pyg-bench commit, runtime image, dataset, competitor + version, raw artifact path. It is **generated** by `scripts/export_docs_numbers.py` in [pyg-bench#109](https://github.com/graphistry/pyg-bench/pull/109) (merged) from artifacts committed there, so regenerating the docs' numbers needs **no GPU box and no benchmark re-run**.
- **`docs/source/_ext/gfql_bench.py`** — a Sphinx extension providing ``:bench:`key```, ``:bench-diag:`key```, `.. bench-provenance::` and `.. bench-disclosures::`. The docs build already runs `-W --keep-going -n`, so a warning is fatal.
- **`bin/check_bench_numbers.py`** — the same gate without Sphinx, plus two checks a docs build cannot make.
- **`docs/test_bench_numbers.py`** — 8 negative tests pinning the rejections.

| Failure | Caught by |
|---|---|
| a key the source of truth does not contain | Sphinx + standalone |
| a run older than `policy.max_age_days` — checked for **every** run, so an incremental build cannot serve an aged-out number | Sphinx + standalone |
| a non-board-quotable cell published as a bare number (it must use `:bench-diag:`) | Sphinx + standalone |
| a page that references a cell without rendering its provenance / disclosures | Sphinx + standalone |
| engine **commit drift** since a published run was measured | standalone only (needs git history) |
| a **hand-typed literal** on a managed page | standalone only |

The disclosure rule is the load-bearing one: a bare ratio stripped of its asterisk launders the caveat, which is worse than manual transcription.

## Scope discipline

**No editorial rewriting, no restructuring, no voice changes.** Where a sentence mixed a withdrawn number with surviving prose, only the numeric clause was removed and the surrounding wording kept. `performance.rst` keeps its existing sections and gains one factual section describing how a number now gets published; it publishes **no new figures**. The provenance-carrying q1–q9 board that #1806 added, and the prose rewrite around it, are deliberately **not** here — they need editorial judgement and are in the follow-up PR.

Known follow-ups, deliberately out of scope: `demos/gfql/benchmark_filter_pagerank_cpu_gpu.ipynb` renders the same withdrawn pipeline figures from the same missing results directory; `benchmark_graphframes.rst` is verifiable but not yet gated.

items.title: Refuse to report benchmark numbers from a run that measured failures
items.body:
Follow-up to #279, fixing a class of hole I found in my own code just as that PR merged.

## The problem

A failed call is small, fast, and cheap to serve — so it **improves every axis the benchmark tracks**. A 500 on `/api/ingredients` would have turned 126,263 bytes into a few hundred, and `--fail-on-regression` would have reported a 99% improvement and exited 0.

Three instances, all the same shape:

| | what happened | why it was invisible |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **REST non-2xx** | recorded as a real measurement | the report tagged the status in the label, but nothing failed |
| **MCP tool errors** | recorded as a smaller payload | a failed tool returns HTTP **200** with `isError` on the result |
| **`recipes/{id}`** | 404 on any remote run | the path hard-coded the fixture's recipe id, which exists only in-process |

The third meant `--url` mode — the whole point of which is real-world numbers — was silently timing an error page for that endpoint.

## The fix

`McpCallResult.IsToolError` detects the MCP case. The recipe id is resolved from `/api/recipes?page=1&pageSize=1`, which is valid in both modes and deterministic in-process (the list order is fixed by the fixture's timestamps). A run that hits any failure prints what failed and **exits 3** without comparing against the baseline:

```text
This run measured failed calls, so its numbers are not comparable:
  GET /api/pantry-does-not-exist (pantry) returned HTTP 404
```

Exit codes are now **1** regression, **2** bad arguments, **3** invalid run.

## Verification

Pointed an endpoint at a missing path and confirmed exit 3 with the offending call named, then reverted. `dotnet test Kotlet.slnx` — 419 passed, 0 failed. Two consecutive clean runs produce identical bytes and query counts.

## One number moved

Resolving the recipe id changes *which* recipe is measured — the list is ordered by update time, so it resolves to the last fixture recipe rather than the first, and that one has no `sourceUrl`. `recipes/{id}` goes 2,413 → 2,399 bytes, and the API total 148,705 → 148,691. Baseline re-recorded; schema unchanged, so a v2 baseline still loads.

Closes #51

# #P5-1 — Performance pass

## What this means in plain English

We measured how fast Claude Lens starts up on a real, months-old chat history (about 200 sessions, 5,500 messages, 83 MB of transcripts). The success criteria were four yes/no questions:

1. **First launch (cold boot): under 1 second.** Measured: **0.29 s** — opens in a third of a second. Pass.
2. **Second launch (warm boot, with cache): under 100 ms.** Measured: **60 ms** — basically instant. Pass.
3. **The cache is actually helping.** The second run is about 1/5 the time of the first. Cache is real, working, and verified. Pass.
4. **Memory usage stays reasonable.** Target: under 500 MB. Measured: **230 MB**. Comfortably inside the design's "low hundreds of MB" band. Pass.

Everything cleared, so **no profiling or production-code changes were needed** — the design is already fast enough on this size of corpus. The whole point of the exercise was to record the numbers, confirm the cache trick works, and leave a row behind for the next person to compare against as the data grows.

---

## Numbers (3-run median against real `~/.claude/projects`)

| Metric | #P2-7 baseline | #P5-1 (this PR) | Change | Target band |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cold boot | 0.21s | **0.29s** | +38% (corpus grew 4136→5541 calls, +34%) | < 1s ✓ |
| Warm boot | 0.03s | **0.06s** | 2× (absolute 60ms still near-instant) | < 100ms ✓ |
| RSS | 179.2MB | **230.6MB** | +29% (proportional to call count) | < 500MB ✓ |
| Data size | (not recorded) | 83.3MB · 128 sessions / 5541 calls | — | — |
| Warm/cold ratio | 0.14× | **0.20×** | cache hit verified | — |

All three target-band thresholds cleared. **No profiling required** per §5.7.

## What changed

`server/ingest/benchmark.ts` (tooling only — no production code path touched in the original push):

- **Data-size column**: total bytes of T (transcript) JSONL across the scan roots, excluding `.cost.jsonl` / `.turn-boundaries.jsonl` sidecars and the root-level `cost-log.jsonl`. Uses `classifyPath` (the path-aware classifier `discover` uses) to stay consistent with the pipeline's own classification and keep both classifiers in lockstep.
- **`--roots <path>` flag**: uses a shared `parseRootsFlag` helper that also lives in `server/cli.ts`, so the two consumers can't drift.
- **Output**: prints the data size, cold/warm breakdown with warm/cold ratio, and a ready-to-paste Markdown row.

`specs/claude-lens-plan.md`:
- Filled in the #P5-1 row of the benchmark log.
- Flipped the `#P5-1` checkbox from `[ ]` to `[x]`.

## Verification

- `npm run verify` (typecheck + lint + format + 1624 vitest tests) — green on the pre-push hook on both the original push and the round-2 fixes commit.
- `npm run bench:ingest` run 3× in a row; numbers stable to ±0.02s on cold boot, ±0.06s on warm boot, ±10MB on RSS. Data size / session count / call count identical across runs. Re-run after the round-2 fixes produced the same numbers (cold 0.29s / warm 0.06s / warm-cold 0.20x).
- Warm-cache hit verified: warm boot is ~5× faster than cold (`(warm/cold ratio: 0.20x)`) and would be ~1× if any file had been touched between cold and warm.
- `parseRootsFlag` smoke-tested against 7 arg shapes (inline, positional, repeats, mixed with other flags, bare flag, empty inline, empty argv) — byte-equivalent to the original cli.ts inline parsing.

## §5.7 follow-up

Single-threaded model confirmed sufficient — no worker pool introduced. If a future corpus reaches 10× the current size, this is the row to revisit; for now the boot is bounded by ~150 MB/s of single-threaded parse throughput.

## Review fixes (round 2)

The [review report](./CODE-REVIEW-PR-117.md) found 0 Critical, 0 High, 2 Medium, 6 Low. **All 7 addressed in the round-2 commit (`cba9dc6`):**

- **🟡 Medium** — `measureDataSize` outer `catch` on `fg` now `console.warn`s once per root (mirrors `discover.ts:163-170` so a misconfigured root is visible to operators, not silently dropped).

items.title: docs(gfql): print the benchmark numbers pyg-bench publishes, and re-verify them
items.body:
**Do not merge without human review.**

Supersedes #1813, which the owner redirected: *"i don't get why this big file is here when we also have docs/source/_ext/gfql_bench.py. more broadly, why is this different from the pyg-bench stuff? should all that be there, and all we do is pretty print their latest json? and if we have any boundary needs, ensure there are data contract tests that run on the pyg-bench side, and we re-verify on our side?"*

This is the consuming half of that factoring. The producing half is pyg-bench graphistry/pyg-bench#113 (merged) and graphistry/pyg-bench#114.

| | #1813 | here |
|---|---|---|
| gate | `bin/check_bench_numbers.py`, 266 lines | none — the rules live in pyg-bench |
| extension | 347 + 420 lines across two modules | 1 module |
| data | generated JSON, unversioned shape | vendored artifact + vendored contract |

## What this adds

- `docs/source/_data/gfql_benchmarks.json` — a vendored copy of pyg-bench's `published/docs-numbers.json`.
- `docs/source/_data/gfql_benchmarks.contract.json` — a vendored copy of the contract it satisfies.
- `docs/source/_ext/gfql_bench.py` — resolves `:bench:` / `:bench-diag:`, renders `bench-provenance` / `bench-disclosures`, and re-verifies the contract before rendering anything.
- `docs/test_bench_numbers.py` — the same checks in the ordinary test lane.

Build failures, never silent text: a key that is not published; a run measured longer ago than `policy.max_age_days`; a non-quotable cell printed as a bare number; a page that drops a referenced number's provenance or disclosures; any contract violation at all. Each of those has a test that watches it fail.

The re-verification is written against the contract **document**, independently of pyg-bench's implementation. A shared library would fail identically on both sides of the boundary and the re-verification would prove nothing.

## `benchmark_filter_pagerank.rst`

Its figures came from a chart generator reading `plans/gfql-gpu-pagerank-benchmark/results/` — a path that has never existed in any commit, and `plans/` is gitignored, so nobody could re-derive them. pyg-bench ported the runners unchanged and re-ran them on dgx-spark under the perf lock against pygraphistry `49db91cc`, with the raw artifacts committed.

| | Neo4j + GDS | GFQL CPU | GFQL GPU | GPU vs Neo4j |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Twitter (2.4M edges) | 11.72 s | 1.58 s | 0.24 s | **49.5x** |
| GPlus (30M edges) | did not complete | 32.10 s | 2.42 s | — |

Every arm reproduces the earlier run's final subgraphs exactly, node for node and edge for edge. The old "46x" measures 49.5x now. The old GPlus ">56x" is gone: that arm lost its connection mid-transaction and never reached a timed run, and a ratio against a run that did not finish is not a speedup.

The two lifecycle SVGs are removed. They render the withdrawn figures as glyph paths and their generator cannot be run.

## Verification

- `docs/ci.sh` run locally (Dockerised Sphinx): **build succeeded**, extension live, table and provenance render. A docs-only diff skips `test-docs` in CI (it `needs: python-lint-types`), so green CI would not have proven the docs built.
- `pytest docs/test_bench_numbers.py` — 13 passed.
- ruff clean on both new files. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` untouched.

## Not in scope

The hand-typed-literal guard over `policy.managed_docs` is not here; it would collide with the factual-correction PR currently touching `performance.rst` / `engines.rst`. Worth a follow-up once those land. `demos/gfql/benchmark_filter_pagerank_cpu_gpu.ipynb` still restates the withdrawn Twitter figures (13.51 s / 45x) and needs the same treatment.

items.title: bench: first real benchmark numbers from summitt-cloud, plus five defects that blocked them
items.body:
## What this is

The benchmark harness added under P2-8 / O7 was validated **offline only** — its README said *"no numbers are committed until a real run produces them"*, and none had been. `benchmarks/results/` was empty and `benchmark_results` held one 2026-07-12 run covering q01–q07, so every query shape added since (q12, q13, q15) and every BI Engine column had **no data at all**.

This is that run, against `summitt-cloud.repath_bench` (1 732 954 step rows / 60 000 trajectories): **210 jobs, zero errors**, promoted to `benchmarks/baselines/`. Full report: [`docs/review/2026-07-25-query-benchmark-run.md`](docs/review/2026-07-25-query-benchmark-run.md).

## The result: the snapshot works, the live TVF is plan-bound

The same detail document, two ways:

| | q04 (live TVF) | q07 (snapshot) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| p95, 1–10 steps | 4209 ms | **357 ms** |
| p95, 200+ steps | 8185 ms | **865 ms** |
| stages | 54–58 | **1–2** |
| avg slot-ms | ~220 000 | **~80** |

~2900× the slot cost for the same answer on similar bytes (~110 MiB both). The cost is assembly, not I/O — so **q04 is the suite's only budget breach**, and it breaches in all four size buckets against the §2.6 sub-second claim. q07 stays under 1 s everywhere.

Also: clustering is worth **29.6–36.4×** in bytes, and the designed `q05`/`q13` pair confirms predicates **prune the scan** rather than being applied after assembly.

**The 20 % regression gate fires twice; neither is a regression.** q04's slot-ms went *down* (244 555 → 218 422) and bytes down while wall-clock rose, and per-iteration slot-ms swings 116 748–337 100 for identical work (same 57–58 stages, same bytes). On-demand slot contention. Read work metrics before latency when the gate fires.

## Five defects fixed — each would have produced *wrong* numbers, not no numbers

1. **`.env` silently overrode explicit environment** in all three scripts. `set -a; source` assigns unconditionally, so `DATASET_ID=repath_bench bash …` ran against the **production** dataset named in `.env`. Worst in `generate_volume.sh`, which *writes* synthetic rows into the primary table and whose own header says "never production", and in `bi_engine_ab.sh`, where it would size **paid capacity** against an unintended dataset.
2. **`BENCH_PROFILE` was dead code** — defaults ran before the preset `case`, so `quick`/`deep` both silently ran the `full` shape.
3. **q12 errored on every iteration** — references `model_pricing_effective`, never deployed to the bench dataset. Deployed there.
4. **The engine-side cross-check was skipped entirely** on a missing permission. `JOBS_BY_PROJECT` needs project-level `bigquery.jobs.listAll`; now falls back to `JOBS_BY_USER`, which needs no grant and returns the same rows since the harness runs every job as the caller. It independently confirms the client-side numbers (q04 200+: 8877 ms engine-side vs 8185 ms client-side).
5. **Failure logs pointed at an always-empty file** — `bq --format=json` prints query errors on *stdout*, redirected to `/dev/null`, so `<job>.stderr` was empty for exactly the failures worth reading.

## Honest limits (recorded, not glossed)

- **BI Engine is NOT measured.** No reservation was created, `bi_engine_mode` is NULL on all 210 jobs, and the `studio.md` ruling is neither confirmed nor revised. Verified afterwards that `BI_CAPACITIES` is empty and no reservation exists — nothing is billing.
- **q06 is the brute-force path.** The index exists but is `TEMPORARILY DISABLED` at 0 % coverage: BigQuery declines to index a base table under 10 GiB and this one is 3.3 GiB. Deploying the index cannot fix it; it needs volume.
- **q14 skips** for want of a content plane (`gcs_payloads`), which the README treats as a valid deployment.
- **The default `WINDOWS=7` would have measured an empty window** — the synthetic volume ends 2026-07-11, so q05/q06/q12/q13/q15 would have reported the latency of aggregating zero rows. This run used `WINDOWS="30 90 365"`; the README now warns about the trap.
- **n=5 per cell**, so a single p95 is one sample. Treat single-cell deltas as noise unless slot-ms and bytes move with them.

`benchmarks/results/<run_id>/` stays gitignored (9.8 MB of raw Jobs API documents); the promoted `summary.json` and the report carry the numbers.

## Follow-ups

- **q04 is the actionable finding** — 54–58 stages for a 7-step trajectory is a plan problem the snapshot path already avoids.
- **BI Engine remains unsettled**; the prerequisite argument stands (over `trajectory_steps_compacted` the R15 dedup is a provable no-op, and its window function is what blocks acceleration).
- Raise volume past 10 GiB for an index-backed q06.
- `smoke_164444` / `pre_171706` are throwaway runs from this session that reached the append-only table; `smoke_164444` carries 3 q12 error rows and empty-window timings. Filter by `run_id`, or purge those two ids.

items.body:
Follow-up to a documentation/website/UX review of the current version. The theme throughout: numbers and status claims were maintained in several places at once and had drifted apart after the 1.4/1.5 releases. This PR removes the duplication so each fact has one source of truth, and fixes the technical issues the review surfaced.

## Benchmark numbers: one source of truth

- `docs/proof-and-benchmarks.md` and `README.md` no longer quote their own (stale, mutually inconsistent) copies of the e2e workflow medians — they link the checked report `benchmarks/e2e-workflow/results/latest.md` and `docs/benchmark-e2e-workflow.md` instead.
- The website compare page derives its medians from `site/app/data/bench.ts`, which the existing `verify-site-bench-data.mjs` guard already asserts against the checked report — so the previously drifted "174 ms / 2254 ms" cells can no longer go stale. Hero/ProofStrip ratios come from the same guarded data.
- Fixed the compare criterion label (the cited numbers are from the realistic corpus, not the small one) and the Ferrocat version note (2.2.0, matching the pinned crate).

## ADR trees merged

`docs/adr/` (001/002, added 2026-07-22) collided with the canonical `adr/` series (001–016), claimed canonical status in parallel, and was never published to the website — the hosted CLI plugin API pages linked into a void. The plugin ADRs are now `adr/017` and `adr/018`, `DECISIONS.md` indexes them, links on the API pages resolve to live `/decisions/*` routes, and hardcoded "16 ADRs" counts were either removed or (on the site) derived at build time.

## Website fixes

- **Missing page metadata (SEO):** ~120 of 126 prerendered routes had no `<title>`, description, canonical, or OG tags. items.title: Fix benchmark commentary that contradicts the rendered figures
items.body:
Fixes two statements in the data.table lab that contradict the published output.

**The problem.** The "Reading this result" callout under the first benchmark
figure states that dplyr is the fastest on time. On the currently published page
the figure shows the opposite — data.table 96.1 ms vs dplyr 191 ms. I wrote that
prose from a render on my own laptop, where dplyr *was* faster (87.4 ms vs
114.8 ms). Comparing the two renders, data.table's time is similar on both
machines while the single-threaded engines are ~2x slower on yours, which flips
the ranking. Memory moved too (dplyr 131 MB here vs 153 MB there).

The nearby callout under the data-generation chunk made this worse by promising
that "only the benchmark timings will differ ... the data and the results will
not".

**The fix.** Both passages are now ordering-agnostic, so they stay true whoever
renders them:

- The benchmark callout keeps the claim that survives across machines
  (data.table's memory advantage) and explains that the *time* ranking depends on
  core count, per-core speed and package versions.
- The data callout now separates the **data and analysis results** (identical
  everywhere, fixed seed) from the **benchmark numbers** (hardware- and
  version-dependent, ranking included).

**Please re-render.** This is a **source-only** commit — I deliberately left
`_freeze/` untouched. Because the freeze stores the executed markdown (prose
included), the new text will not appear on the site until someone re-renders. I
did not re-render myself so that the published benchmark numbers stay yours rather
than being replaced by my laptop's, which read less clearly for students. A
`quarto render labs/datatable/index.qmd` on your machine will pick up the new
wording and keep your numbers.
